job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Ivan Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I take the tram to Fairmont Foods, a food distributor, where I'm a junior buyer: comparing supplier quotes, drafting emails and booking deliveries, with an AI assistant open on one screen all day. I did business and economics at university and passed, with no internships, and I rent a flat with two friends. In the evenings I run a small online shop that sells imported spices, and my mum, who is a nurse, rolls her eyes at how many projects I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fewer headaches, and let's keep building things anyway. At work I'd tell my team the tools we have are enough to be useful, and we should keep trimming the boring parts. Online I'd post a few tips and not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit let down. I use AI every day to compare supplier quotes and draft purchase emails, and I've already saved my team hours. If the whole wave stalls, my head start matters less, but my job is secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as a junior buyer at Fairmont Foods, a food distributor, and keep building little spreadsheets and scripts that make the team faster. I'd keep the online shop I run for imported spices, which made 220 last month. I'd put 200 a month into a cheap index fund after paying my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Not a care in the world about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the spice shop start, and what does it teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, Amina, is a nurse, and she thinks I take on too many things. She'd say stick with one job. I'd tell her the spice shop is practice for running something real, and she'd roll her eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about all the side projects?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools don't improve, I'd just keep doing what I'm doing and add a second supplier line to the shop. What I like about a plateau is that I can plan around it. No surprises.

I'd tell my team the tools we have are **enough** to be useful.
think: I'd be a little **let down**, because a stalled wave shrinks my head start.
My own job is **secure**, so I'm not worried.
do: Keep building **spreadsheets and scripts** that speed up the buying team.
Run the **spice shop**, which made 220 last month.
Put **200 a month** into a cheap index fund after the loan.
feel: I'd feel **good**, with no worries about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board now, because this is the most useful change since the spreadsheet. At work I'd offer to build tools for the whole buying team. Online I'd write about how a junior can use the tools to do senior work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is in the middle of it, because buying, comparing quotes and booking deliveries are on the list. But I'm the person doing the automating, so I think I come out ahead. The risk is that once I automate my own work, I've shown them they need fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fairmont's head of buying, Lena, to give me a six-month project to automate the quote comparisons. I'd put the savings in numbers and ask for a raise at the end. I'd grow the spice shop and try to add two more products, and I'd put 300 a month into the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a small voice at the back asking if I'm sawing off my own branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you manage the risk of automating yourself out of a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The way I'd manage that is simple. I'd always want to be one step ahead of the tool, so I'm needed to run what I built. I'd also learn the data side, which is where the pay goes. I'd tell mum I'm not worried, and mostly I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fallback look like if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it went badly, I'd have the shop and the savings. A few hundred a month from the shop and a 300 savings habit would keep me going for a while. And I could live with my mum in Rosedale for a few months.

fieldNote: Ivan sees himself as **ahead of the tool**, though he knows automating his own tasks could cut team numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and the rules need to change fast. At work I'd push the company to share the gains with staff. Online I'd back ideas like a basic income, because I can't see an alternative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is toast in two years. Buying is thinking work, and a system that does it better and cheaper doesn't need a junior buyer. Being good with the tools just means I see it coming first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell part of my small index fund, about 1,500, and put it into the spice shop, to build it into something real before the job ends. I'd learn how to source and ship directly, and open a second shop with a friend, Tariq. I'd cut my rent by moving to a cheaper room and save every spare pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit alive, if that makes sense. It's like standing on the edge before a jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the edge your shop could keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop might not survive either, because AI shops will compete with mine. The only edge I'd have is trust and personal contact with suppliers. I'd also have a three-year head start on robots in the warehouse. I'd lean into the physical side, importing, packing, shipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you give the shop up for a steady job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would tell me to take any steady job, and she'd be right. If the shop wasn't working by month eight, I'd take a warehouse or logistics job to pay the bills, and learn that business from inside.

I'd back ideas like **basic income**, since I can't see an alternative.
think: My job is **toast** in two years, because buying is thinking work.
The shop could also be hit if **AI shops** compete with mine.
do: Move about **1,500** from the index fund into the spice shop.
Open a **second shop** with my friend Tariq and source directly.
Move to a **cheaper room** and save every spare pound.
feel: I'd feel **worried** but a bit alive, like standing at the edge before a jump.
S2.quote: The only edge I'd have is trust and personal contact with suppliers.
fieldNote: Ivan expects his **buying job** to go and bets on trust and physical supply for his shop.
His **adaptive** streak shows: he moves money and builds options instead of freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and we'd be wise to use it. At work I'd say let's design our jobs around what the tools can't do. Online I'd talk about ways to use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm okay with it. I'd have five years to build a business and a skill, and I'm someone who starts things. I think the people who suffer most will be those who didn't plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop to cover most of my rent by year two. I'd learn about supply chains and logistics through a part-time diploma, around 2,000. I'd keep working at Fairmont and keep automating, because it makes me valuable until it doesn't. I'd put 300 a month into the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. Five years is a deadline, and I do well with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the June check look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop reached 800 a month by 2029, I'd go full-time on it and a second business. If not, I'd move into logistics, because a hands-on business gets three more years. I'd set myself a check every June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tariq put into the import company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Tariq and I talk about starting a small import company. This is the push we'd need. We'd put in 2,000 each and see what the first year taught us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and people should build things. At work I'd keep delivering and keep learning. Online I'd say this is the best time to start something small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be calm and excited. By 32 I could own a real business, have savings, and be someone who knows both the tools and the trade. Ten years is a lot of tries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for two or three years, finish a diploma, and build the import company on the side. I'd save 400 a month in my later years of work and aim for a deposit by 27. I'd also keep making things that help the team, because they get me noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy, mostly. It's the one that makes me want to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the ideas would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only thing that would hold me back is my own impatience. I'd probably try three ideas, and two would fail, which is fine at 23. Failing small and early is better than failing big and late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does acting as if it's the short version matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm wrong and it comes in five years, I'd still be ahead, because I'd have been building the whole time. That's why I'd act as if the short version were true.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Buying is thinking work, so my job would go and the shop would be hit too, because AI shops compete. What would help is a clear safety net, like a basic income, and room to start businesses cheaply. I'd also want suppliers I know by name.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being good with the tools isn't a shield. It means I see the change a bit sooner than the others. Whoever you are, you still need a plan B and some money.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools isn't a shield.
portrait: Ivan is a business and economics graduate, four months into a junior buyer job, **renting** with friends.
He is centrist and uses AI every day, so he moves early and builds options.
His mood runs from calm to **anxious** as warning shrinks, and he answers with side income and logistics.
He is helped by a nurse mother in Rosedale, but he is **self-reliant** by habit.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most: his buying job would go and his online shop would face AI competitors.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **safety net**, cheap ways to start a business, and supplier relationships he knows by name.
